questions.q: You put on your socks. What do you put on next?
questions.explain: Socks go on first, then shoes go on top of them.
questions.tip: Socks first, shoes second, out the door you go!

questions.q: To plant a seed, what do you do first?
questions.explain: The seed needs a hole in the dirt before it can grow.
questions.tip: Dig, drop, cover, water: dig comes first!

questions.q: First you get in the bath. Then you wash. What comes last?
questions.explain: After washing, you get out and dry off.
questions.tip: In, wash, out, dry: the towel is the finish line.

questions.q: A caterpillar makes a cocoon. What comes out next?
questions.explain: A caterpillar changes inside the cocoon and comes out as a butterfly.
questions.tip: Crawl, wrap, flap: caterpillar, cocoon, butterfly!

questions.q: To make a sandwich, what do you do last?
questions.explain: You make the sandwich first and eat it at the end.
questions.tip: The yummy part is always the last part.

questions.q: Snow falls. Then you roll big snowballs. What can you make next?
questions.explain: You stack the snowballs to build a snowman.
questions.tip: Roll, stack, smile: hello, snowman!

questions.q: You open the door and walk through. What do you do next?
questions.explain: After you walk through, you close the door behind you.
questions.tip: Open, walk, close: like a door sandwich.

questions.q: Red, blue, red, blue, red. What comes next?
questions.explain: The colors take turns: red, then blue, over and over.
questions.tip: Say it like a song: red-blue, red-blue!

questions.q: Clap, stomp, clap, stomp, clap. What comes next?
questions.explain: Clap and stomp take turns, so stomp comes after clap.
questions.tip: Do it with your body: clap your hands, stomp your feet!

questions.q: Circle, square, circle, square. What comes next?
questions.explain: The shapes take turns, and the last one was square, so circle is next.
questions.tip: Round, pointy, round, pointy: like a wheel then a box.

questions.q: Cat, dog, dog, cat, dog, dog, cat. What comes next?
questions.explain: The pattern is one cat, then two dogs. After cat comes dog.
questions.tip: Meow, woof, woof! Meow, woof, woof!

questions.q: Big, small, big, small. What comes next?
questions.explain: Big and small take turns, and small was last, so big is next.
questions.tip: Say it loud then soft: BIG, small, BIG, small!

questions.q: Sun, moon, sun, moon. What comes next?
questions.explain: Sun and moon take turns, just like day and night.
questions.tip: Day, night, day, night: the sky has a pattern too!

questions.q: Apple, banana, apple, banana, apple. What comes next?
questions.explain: Apple and banana take turns, so banana comes after apple.
questions.tip: Crunch, peel, crunch, peel!

questions.q: A ball rolls off the table. Which way does it fall?
questions.explain: Things fall down to the floor.
questions.tip: What goes up must come down, and balls love the floor!

questions.q: Up is the opposite of what?
questions.explain: Up and down are opposites.
questions.tip: Point to the sky for up and to your toes for down.

questions.q: Left is the opposite of what?
questions.explain: Left and right are opposites.
questions.tip: Wave your left hand, then your right hand: two sides!

questions.q: A bird flies high into the sky. Is it going up or down?
questions.explain: The sky is up above us.
questions.tip: Birds go up, up, up to say hi to the clouds.

questions.q: You climb the ladder and then go down the slide. Which way do you slide?
questions.explain: Slides take you down to the ground.
questions.tip: Wheee goes down!

questions.q: A robot steps right, then steps left. Where is it now?
questions.explain: One step right and one step left cancel out.
questions.tip: Right then left is like a little dance back home.

questions.q: A robot is facing a door. To get to the door, should it go forward or backward?
questions.explain: Forward means the way you are facing.
questions.tip: Forward is where your nose points!

questions.q: To wash your hands: get them wet, use soap, then what?
questions.explain: After soap, you rinse it off and dry your hands.
questions.tip: Wet, soap, rinse, dry: bubbles say bye-bye!

questions.q: First you put on your coat. Then you zip it up. What did you do first?
questions.explain: The word first tells you: the coat goes on before the zip.
questions.tip: You cannot zip air: coat first!

questions.q: To build a tower, which block goes first?
questions.explain: Towers are built from the bottom up.
questions.tip: Start at the floor and grow tall like a tree.

questions.q: To read a book, what do you do first?
questions.explain: You must open a book before you can read it.
questions.tip: Open the cover like opening a door to a story.

questions.q: Simon says: touch your nose, then touch your toes. What do you touch second?
questions.explain: Nose was first, then toes came second.
questions.tip: Nose, toes: it even rhymes!

questions.q: To draw a smiley face: draw a circle, add eyes, then add what?
questions.explain: A smiley face needs a smile at the end.
questions.tip: Circle, eyes, smile: now it smiles back at you!

questions.q: A robot follows steps. What order does it use?
questions.explain: Robots and computers do steps in the exact order they are given.
questions.tip: Robots are great listeners: step one, step two, step three.

questions.q: What is an algorithm?
choices: A list of steps to do a job
questions.explain: An algorithm is a set of steps in order, like a recipe.
questions.tip: An algorithm is a recipe for a computer.

questions.q: What is the first step to make toast?
questions.explain: The bread must be toasted before you butter or eat it.
questions.tip: Bread in, pop up, butter, munch!

questions.q: How does a computer follow instructions?
questions.explain: Computers do exactly what the steps say, even if the steps are wrong.
questions.tip: A computer is like a very literal friend: it does just what you say.

questions.q: Steps to brush teeth: put paste on the brush, brush your teeth, rinse. What is step 2?
questions.explain: Brushing comes in the middle, after the paste and before rinsing.
questions.tip: Paste, brush, rinse: one, two, three, sparkly teeth!

questions.q: Why do steps for a computer need to be very clear?
choices: Computers cannot guess what you mean
questions.explain: A computer cannot fill in missing steps, so every step must be spelled out.
questions.tip: Give a computer a map with every turn, not just "go to the park".

questions.q: Lemonade: squeeze lemons, add water, add sugar, stir. What is the last step?
questions.explain: Stirring mixes everything together at the end.
questions.tip: Squeeze, pour, sweeten, swirl!

questions.q: Which is a good instruction for a robot?
questions.explain: Good instructions say exactly what to do and how much.
questions.tip: Robots need numbers, not nice ideas.

questions.q: Planting: dig a hole, drop in a seed, cover it with dirt, water it. What comes after dropping in the seed?
questions.explain: The seed gets tucked in with dirt before you water it.
questions.tip: Tuck the seed in bed with a dirt blanket.

questions.q: Who writes the instructions that computers follow?
questions.explain: Programmers, also called coders, write the steps for computers.
questions.tip: Coders are the bosses who tell computers what to do.

questions.q: A recipe is like an algorithm because...
questions.explain: Both a recipe and an algorithm are step-by-step instructions.
questions.tip: Cooks follow recipes; computers follow algorithms.

questions.q: "Repeat 3 times: clap." How many claps?
questions.explain: Repeat 3 times means do it 3 times: clap, clap, clap.
questions.tip: Repeat is like an echo that counts.

questions.q: "Repeat 2 times: jump, then clap." How many jumps?
questions.explain: Each time through you jump once, and you go through 2 times.
questions.tip: Jump-clap, jump-clap: two jumps in the dance.

questions.q: "Repeat 2 times: jump, then clap." How many moves in all?
questions.explain: Jump, clap, jump, clap is 4 moves.
questions.tip: Two moves, done twice, makes four. 2 + 2 = 4!

questions.q: Instead of "step, step, step, step," what is a shorter way to say it?
questions.explain: A loop says the step once and how many times to do it.
questions.tip: Loops are lazy in a smart way: say it once, do it lots.

questions.q: What is a loop in coding?
choices: Doing the same steps again and again
questions.explain: A loop repeats steps, so you do not have to write them over and over.
questions.tip: A loop goes round and round like a merry-go-round.

questions.q: "Repeat 5 times: stomp." You stomped 3 times. How many more stomps?
questions.explain: 5 minus 3 is 2 more stomps.
questions.tip: Count up from 3 on your fingers: 4, 5. Two more!

questions.q: A robot draws a square: "Repeat 4 times: move, turn." Why 4?
questions.explain: Each move draws one side, and a square has 4 sides.
questions.tip: Four sides, four corners, four repeats.

questions.q: "Repeat 3 times: hop." Then "clap one time." How many hops?
questions.explain: Only the hop is inside the repeat, so you hop 3 times and clap once.
questions.tip: Only what is inside the loop goes round and round.

questions.q: Why do coders use loops?
choices: To save writing the same step many times
questions.explain: Loops make programs shorter and easier to change.
questions.tip: Why write it ten times when you can loop it?

questions.q: "If it is raining, take an umbrella." It is raining. What do you do?
questions.explain: The if part is true, so you do the then part.
questions.tip: If it rains, umbrella reigns!

questions.q: "If it is raining, take an umbrella." It is sunny. Do you take the umbrella?
questions.explain: The if part is false, so you skip the then part.
questions.tip: No rain, no umbrella: the if says no.

questions.q: "If the light is red, stop." The light is red. What do you do?
questions.explain: The light is red, so the rule says stop.
questions.tip: Red means stop, like a stop sign.

questions.q: "If you are cold, wear a jacket. If not, wear a T-shirt." You are warm. What do you wear?
questions.explain: You are not cold, so you follow the "if not" part.
questions.tip: If chooses a path: cold goes one way, warm goes the other.

questions.q: "If the dog is hungry, feed it." The dog just ate a big meal. Do you feed it?
questions.explain: The dog is not hungry, so the if part is false.
questions.tip: Check the if first, like checking the dog bowl.

questions.q: "If the card shows 5, clap. If not, stomp." The card shows 3. What do you do?
questions.explain: 3 is not 5, so you stomp.
questions.tip: Not a match? Take the other path!

questions.q: A game says: "If you touch the lava, you lose." What makes you lose?
questions.explain: The if rule only cares about touching the lava.
questions.tip: The floor is lava: the if is watching your feet!

questions.q: Which one is an if-then rule?
choices: If it is dark, turn on the light
questions.explain: An if-then rule says what to do when something is true.
questions.tip: If-then rules start with "if" and tell you what to do.

questions.q: An if rule makes the computer...
questions.explain: If rules let a program make choices.
questions.tip: If is a fork in the road: the computer picks a path.

questions.q: What is a bug in a program?
questions.explain: A bug is an error that makes a program do the wrong thing.
questions.tip: In 1947 a real moth got stuck in a computer, and the team taped it in their notebook as an actual bug!

questions.q: Steps: put on shoes, then put on socks. What is wrong?
choices: Socks should go on before shoes
questions.explain: The steps are in the wrong order.
questions.tip: Socks on top of shoes would look silly!

questions.q: Finding and fixing mistakes in code is called...
questions.explain: De-bugging means taking the bugs out.
questions.tip: De-bug: shoo the bug out of your code!

questions.q: Steps: eat cereal, pour milk, get a bowl. Which step should be first?
questions.explain: You need a bowl before you can pour or eat.
questions.tip: No bowl means cereal on the table!

questions.q: A robot needs to move 3 steps to the cookie, but the code says "move 2." How do you fix it?
questions.explain: The number was wrong, so you change it to the right number.
questions.tip: Count the squares, then fix the number.

questions.q: Steps for a letter: mail it, write it, put it in an envelope. Which step should be last?
questions.explain: Write it, put it in the envelope, then mail it.
questions.tip: You cannot mail a letter you have not written yet!

questions.q: Your robot turned left, but it should turn right. What should you do?
questions.explain: The robot did what the steps said, so you fix the step.
questions.tip: Fix the steps, not the robot.

questions.q: Your code has a bug. What is a good first thing to do?
choices: Go through the steps one at a time
questions.explain: Checking each step helps you find where it goes wrong.
questions.tip: Be a detective: check each clue one by one.

questions.q: Snowman steps: put on the head, then roll the body. What is the bug?
choices: The body should come before the head
questions.explain: The head needs a body to sit on, so the order is wrong.
questions.tip: Build from the bottom up, like a snowman sandwich.

questions.q: What do you use to type letters?
questions.explain: A keyboard has keys with letters and numbers.
questions.tip: Keyboard has keys, like a piano for words.

questions.q: Which part shows pictures and words?
questions.explain: The screen, or monitor, shows what the computer is doing.
questions.tip: The screen is the computer's face.

questions.q: What do you move and click to point at things?
questions.explain: A mouse moves the pointer on the screen.
questions.tip: A computer mouse has a long cord tail, like a real mouse.

questions.q: Which part lets you hear sounds?
questions.explain: Speakers play music and sounds.
questions.tip: Speakers speak!

questions.q: What makes paper copies of your work?
questions.explain: A printer puts words and pictures on paper.
questions.tip: A printer prints on paper.

questions.q: Someone you do not know asks online where you live. What should you do?
choices: Send a picture of your house
Not tell, and tell a grown-up
questions.explain: Never share where you live online. A grown-up can help.
questions.tip: Your address stays at home, not on the internet.

questions.q: Should you share your password with your friends?
choices: No, only with a parent or trusted grown-up
questions.explain: Passwords keep your stuff safe, so keep them private.
questions.tip: A password is like a toothbrush: do not share it!

questions.q: A pop-up says "You won a prize! Click here!" What should you do?
questions.explain: Prize pop-ups are often tricks. Ask a grown-up.
questions.tip: If it sounds too good to be true, it is a trick.

questions.q: Something online makes you feel scared or upset. What should you do?
questions.explain: A trusted grown-up can help you, and you will not be in trouble.
questions.tip: Uh-oh feeling? Tell a grown-up.

questions.q: Is it okay to say mean things to people online?
questions.explain: Real people read what you write, so be kind.
questions.tip: Type like the person is right next to you.

questions.q: In Scratch, a script under "when green flag clicked" starts when...
questions.explain: The green flag is the go button for Scratch projects.
questions.tip: Green means go, just like a traffic light.

questions.q: In Scratch, what is a sprite?
choices: A character or object that can move and act
questions.explain: Sprites are the characters, like the Scratch cat.
questions.tip: Sprites are the actors; the stage is where they perform.

questions.q: What is an event in programming?
choices: Something that happens, like a click or key press, that starts code
questions.explain: Events trigger code to run.
questions.tip: An event is a doorbell: when it rings, the code answers.

questions.q: "move 10 steps" runs, then "move 10 steps" runs again. How far did the sprite move?
questions.explain: 10 plus 10 is 20 steps.
questions.tip: Steps add up, like walking down a hallway.

questions.q: Which block makes a sprite show a speech bubble?
questions.explain: The say block shows words in a speech bubble.
questions.tip: Say blocks make sprites talk, like a comic strip.

questions.q: "when space key pressed" is an example of what?
questions.explain: It waits for something to happen, then runs code.
questions.tip: Hat-shaped blocks sit on top and wait for something to happen.

questions.q: In Scratch, the picture behind the sprites on the stage is called a...
questions.explain: The stage uses backdrops; sprites use costumes.
questions.tip: Backdrop is the back of the stage, like scenery in a play.

questions.q: Switching a sprite between costumes quickly can make it look like it is...
questions.explain: Fast costume changes make animation, like a flip book.
questions.tip: Costume switching is a flip book for sprites.

questions.q: In Scratch, x tells a sprite's left-right position. What does y tell?
questions.explain: x is left-right and y is up-down.
questions.tip: Y goes to the sky!

questions.q: Why do block languages snap blocks together?
choices: Blocks only fit where they make sense, so there are fewer typing mistakes
questions.explain: Snapping blocks avoids spelling and typing mistakes.
questions.tip: Like puzzle pieces, blocks only fit the right way.

questions.q: "repeat 4: move 50 steps, turn 90 degrees" draws what shape?
questions.explain: Four equal sides with four 90 degree turns make a square.
questions.tip: Four sides, four corners, four repeats: square!

questions.q: To draw a triangle with "repeat 3: move, turn", how many degrees should the sprite turn each time?
questions.explain: The turns must add up to a full circle: 360 divided by 3 is 120.
questions.tip: Any closed shape turns a full 360 in total, so divide 360 by the number of sides.

questions.q: What does a "forever" block do?
choices: Repeats the blocks inside until the program stops
questions.explain: Forever keeps looping until you click the stop sign.
questions.tip: Forever is a hamster wheel that never stops on its own.

questions.q: "repeat 3: (repeat 2: clap)". How many claps?
questions.explain: The inside loop claps 2 times, and that happens 3 times: 3 x 2 = 6.
questions.tip: Loops inside loops multiply.

questions.q: "if touching edge then turn around". When does the sprite turn around?
choices: Only when it touches the edge
questions.explain: The if block only runs its inside blocks when the condition is true.
questions.tip: If is a guard that only opens the gate when the rule is true.

questions.q: An if-else block picks between how many paths?
questions.explain: If the condition is true it takes one path, otherwise the else path.
questions.tip: If-else is a fork in the road with two ways to go.

questions.q: "if score > 10 then say You win! else say Keep going". The score is 10. What does it say?
questions.explain: 10 is not greater than 10, so the else part runs.
questions.tip: Greater than means bigger, and 10 is not bigger than itself.

questions.q: Which task needs a loop?
choices: Making a ball bounce over and over
questions.explain: Over and over is the job of a loop.
questions.tip: If you hear "over and over," think loop.

questions.q: "repeat until touching edge: move 5 steps". When does it stop?
questions.explain: Repeat until keeps going until the condition becomes true.
questions.tip: Repeat until is like "keep walking until you reach the wall."

questions.q: In "if raining and cold", what does "and" mean?
questions.explain: And needs every part to be true.
questions.tip: AND is picky: it wants both. OR is easygoing: one is enough.

questions.q: A variable is like...
choices: A labeled box that holds a value
questions.explain: A variable has a name and stores a value you can change.
questions.tip: A variable is a labeled box you can put things in.

questions.q: score starts at 0. "change score by 1" runs 3 times. What is score?
questions.tip: Each change adds a marble to the box.

questions.q: "set lives to 3", then "change lives by -1". What is lives?
questions.explain: Changing by -1 takes one away: 3 - 1 = 2.
questions.tip: Minus one is like losing a heart in a video game.

questions.q: Why give a variable a good name like "score"?
choices: So people know what it holds
questions.explain: Clear names make code easier to read and fix.
questions.tip: Label your boxes when you move house, and label your variables too.

questions.q: "set x to 5", then "set x to 8". What is x now?
questions.explain: Set replaces the old value, so x is 8.
questions.tip: Set empties the box and puts in something new.

questions.q: Can a variable's value change while a program runs?
choices: Yes, that is why it is called a variable
questions.explain: Variable means "able to vary," or change.
questions.tip: Variable sounds like "vary-able": able to change.

questions.q: "set apples to 4", "change apples by 2", "change apples by 2". What is apples?
questions.tip: Change adds to the box; it does not empty it.

questions.q: "set a to 3", then "set b to a + 2". What is b?
questions.explain: a holds 3, so a + 2 is 5.
questions.tip: Peek in box a, add 2, put the answer in box b.

questions.q: Which is the best variable for a game timer?
questions.explain: A good name tells you what the value means.
questions.tip: Good names are like name tags at a party.

questions.q: Binary numbers use which digits?
questions.explain: Binary has only two digits: 0 and 1.
questions.tip: Bi means two, like a bicycle has two wheels.

questions.q: Why do computers use binary?
choices: Their tiny switches are either off (0) or on (1)
questions.explain: Computer chips are made of millions of tiny on/off switches.
questions.tip: Think of a light switch: off is 0, on is 1.

questions.q: What number is binary 10?
questions.explain: In binary the places are worth 1, 2, 4, 8. So 10 means one 2 and no 1s.
questions.tip: Binary 10 is "two", not "ten": there are 10 kinds of people, those who get it and those who do not!

questions.q: What number is binary 11?
questions.explain: One 2 plus one 1 is 3.
questions.tip: Places from the right are 1, 2, 4, 8: doubling like a growing snack pile.

questions.q: What number is binary 101?
questions.explain: One 4, no 2, one 1: 4 + 1 = 5.
questions.tip: Read places right to left: 1, 2, 4. Add the ones that are on.

questions.q: How do you write 4 in binary?
questions.explain: 4 is one 4, no 2, no 1: 100.
questions.tip: Every power of two in binary is a 1 followed by zeros.

questions.q: A single 0 or 1 is called a...
questions.explain: Bit is short for binary digit.
questions.tip: A bit is a tiny bit of information.

questions.q: How many bits are in a byte?
questions.explain: One byte is a group of 8 bits.
questions.tip: A byte is a big bite: 8 bits in one mouthful.

questions.q: Binary places from the right are worth 1, 2, 4, 8. What number is binary 1000?
questions.explain: Only the 8s place is on, so it is 8.
questions.tip: The 1 sits in the 8 seat.

questions.q: Which password is the strongest?
questions.explain: Long passwords with a mix of words, numbers and symbols are hard to guess.
questions.tip: Make a silly sentence password: long and weird is strong.

questions.q: Who should you share your password with?
choices: Only a parent or trusted grown-up
questions.explain: Even friends could accidentally share it. Keep it with trusted adults.
questions.tip: Passwords are like toothbrushes: do not share them.

questions.q: Which is private information you should not share online?
questions.explain: Your address shows where you live, so keep it private.
questions.tip: Where you live stays off the web.

questions.q: A message says your game account is locked and asks for your password. What is it most likely?
choices: A trick to steal your password
questions.explain: Real companies do not ask for your password in a message.
questions.tip: Anyone asking for your password is fishing for it.

questions.q: Before downloading a new game or app, you should...
questions.explain: Some downloads have viruses or hidden costs.
questions.tip: Ask before you click download.

questions.q: Is everything you read online true?
questions.explain: Anyone can post online, so check facts.
questions.tip: Be a fact detective: check two good sources.

questions.q: Someone online is being mean to you. What should you do?
choices: Do not reply, save it, and tell a trusted adult
questions.explain: Telling an adult gets you help; replying can make it worse.
questions.tip: Stop, save, tell.

questions.q: Why should you log out on a shared computer?
choices: So others cannot use your account
questions.explain: If you stay logged in, the next person could use your account.
questions.tip: Logging out is locking the door behind you.

questions.q: Why is using the same password everywhere risky?
choices: If one is stolen, all your accounts can be opened
questions.explain: One leaked password would unlock everything.
questions.tip: One key for every door means one lost key opens them all.

questions.q: A longer password is usually...
questions.explain: Each extra character makes many more possible passwords.
questions.tip: Longer is stronger.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The + joins the two strings exactly, including the space after the comma.
questions.tip: + on strings is glue: it sticks them together exactly as they are.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: x and y are numbers, so + adds them.
questions.tip: Numbers add, strings stick.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The quotes make them strings, so + joins them instead of adding.
questions.tip: Quotes turn numbers into words, and words just stick together.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: len counts characters: S, a, m.
questions.tip: len is short for length: count the letters.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Python starts counting at 0, so index 0 is the first letter.
questions.tip: Python counts from zero, like floors in a European building.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Multiplying a string by 3 repeats it 3 times.
questions.tip: String times 3 is a string photocopier.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: x starts at 10, then becomes 10 + 5.
questions.tip: The right side is worked out first, then stored in the box on the left.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: // is floor division: it divides and drops the remainder.
questions.tip: Two slashes chop off the leftovers.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: % gives the remainder: 7 divided by 3 is 2 remainder 1.
questions.tip: % is the leftovers after sharing cookies equally.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: .upper() returns the string in capital letters.
questions.tip: upper means UPPERCASE: the letters stand up tall.

questions.q: Which symbol starts a comment in Python?
questions.explain: Python ignores everything after # on a line.
questions.tip: The # is a hashtag note to humans that Python ignores.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: ** is power: 2 x 2 x 2 = 8.
questions.tip: Two stars make it power up.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 12 is not 13 or more, so the else part runs.
questions.tip: Else is the "otherwise" door.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 7 % 2 is 1, not 0, so 7 is odd.
questions.tip: Even numbers share evenly by 2 with nothing left over.

questions.q: Which operator checks if two values are equal in Python?
questions.explain: = stores a value; == compares two values.
questions.tip: One = puts in the box; two == asks "are these the same?"

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 75 is not over 80, but it is over 60, so elif runs.
questions.tip: Python checks top to bottom and stops at the first true one.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: != means "not equal". a and b are both 5, so they are equal.

questions.tip: Recursion on lists: handle the first item, let recursion handle the rest.

questions.q: Which SQL statement reads data from a table?
questions.explain: SELECT retrieves rows; the others change data.
questions.tip: SELECT is shopping: you pick what you want to see.

questions.q: What does this query return?
choices: The names of students older than 18
questions.explain: WHERE filters rows, and SELECT name picks the column.
questions.tip: SELECT picks columns, WHERE picks rows.

questions.q: Which clause sorts query results?
questions.explain: ORDER BY sorts, ascending by default.
questions.tip: ORDER BY puts things in order; GROUP BY puts them in piles.

questions.q: What does COUNT(*) return?
questions.explain: COUNT(*) counts rows, including rows that contain NULLs.
questions.tip: COUNT counts heads in the room.

questions.q: What is a primary key?
choices: A column that uniquely identifies each row
questions.explain: No two rows can share a primary key value.
questions.tip: A primary key is a student ID number: one per person, no repeats.

questions.q: What is a foreign key?
choices: A column that refers to a primary key in another table
A key from another database vendor
questions.explain: Foreign keys link tables together.
questions.tip: A foreign key is a pointer to a row that lives in another table.

questions.q: What does an INNER JOIN return?
choices: Only rows that have a match in both tables
questions.explain: Unmatched rows are left out; outer joins keep them.
questions.tip: INNER JOIN is the overlap in the middle of a Venn diagram.

questions.q: Which clause filters groups after GROUP BY?
questions.explain: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters the groups.
questions.tip: WHERE works before grouping, HAVING works after.

questions.q: What does this statement do?
choices: Deletes every row in the orders table
questions.explain: Without WHERE, DELETE affects every row.
questions.tip: Forget WHERE, lose everywhere.

questions.q: How do you find rows where the email column has no value?
questions.explain: NULL means unknown, so = NULL is never true; use IS NULL.
questions.tip: NULL is not equal to anything, not even itself.

questions.q: Which protocol guarantees reliable, in-order delivery?
questions.explain: TCP uses acknowledgments and retransmits lost data.
questions.tip: TCP is certified mail; UDP is tossing postcards.

questions.q: What is the default port for HTTPS?
questions.explain: HTTP uses 80, SSH uses 22, HTTPS uses 443.
questions.tip: Secure HTTPS gets the bigger number: 443 beats plain old 80.

questions.q: What is the default port for plain HTTP?
questions.explain: Port 80 is the standard unencrypted web port.
questions.tip: 80 is the old-school web door.

questions.q: What does HTTP status 404 mean?
questions.explain: The server could not find the requested resource.
questions.tip: 404: the page went for a walk and did not come back.

questions.q: What does HTTP status 200 mean?
questions.explain: 2xx codes mean success.
questions.tip: 200 is the thumbs-up.

questions.q: Which range of HTTP status codes means a server error?
questions.explain: 4xx is a client error, 5xx is a server error.
questions.tip: 4xx is your fault, 5xx is their fault.

questions.q: How many bits long is an IPv4 address?
questions.explain: IPv4 has four 8-bit numbers, like 192.168.1.1.
questions.tip: Four numbers, each one byte: 4 x 8 = 32.

questions.q: How many bits long is an IPv6 address?
questions.explain: IPv6 was made much bigger to avoid running out of addresses.
questions.tip: IPv6 is four times as long as IPv4.

questions.q: What does the address 127.0.0.1 refer to?
questions.explain: It is the loopback address.
questions.tip: There is no place like 127.0.0.1.

questions.q: What does DNS translate?
choices: IP addresses into MAC addresses only
questions.explain: Your computer asks DNS for the IP behind a name.
questions.tip: DNS is the internet's phone book.

questions.q: What does git commit do?
choices: Records a snapshot of the staged changes in your repository
Uploads your code to a server
questions.explain: Commits are saved locally; push sends them to a remote.
questions.tip: A commit is a save point in a video game.

questions.q: What does git add do?
choices: Stages changes to go into the next commit
questions.explain: Staging lets you choose exactly what goes into a commit.
questions.tip: add puts items in the shopping cart; commit checks out.

questions.q: What does git push do?
choices: Sends your local commits to a remote repository
questions.explain: Push uploads; pull downloads and integrates.
questions.tip: Push sends it out, pull brings it in.

questions.q: What does git pull do?
choices: Fetches changes from a remote and integrates them into your branch
questions.explain: Pull is fetch plus merge (or rebase).
questions.tip: Pull is fetch, then merge: get the mail and open it.

questions.q: What does git clone do?
choices: Copies an existing repository, including its history
questions.explain: Clone gives you a full local copy to work in.
questions.tip: Clone is a full photocopy of the project and its diary.

questions.q: What is a branch in git?
choices: A separate line of development that points to a commit
questions.explain: Branches let you work on features without touching main.
questions.tip: A branch is a parallel universe for your code.

questions.q: When does a merge conflict happen?
choices: Two branches change the same lines in different ways
questions.explain: Git cannot pick which change wins, so you decide.
questions.tip: Two people edited the same sentence, and git asks you to referee.

questions.q: What does git status show?
choices: Which files are changed, staged or untracked
questions.explain: Status is a snapshot of your working directory and staging area.
questions.tip: git status is checking your bag before you leave.

questions.q: What does git log show?
questions.explain: Log lists commits with authors, dates and messages.
questions.tip: git log is the project's diary.

questions.q: What is a .gitignore file for?
choices: Listing files git should not track
questions.explain: Build output, secrets and temporary files often go in .gitignore.
questions.tip: .gitignore is a "do not pack" list.

questions.q: What is phishing?
choices: A fake message that tricks you into giving up passwords or money
A kind of computer virus scanner
questions.explain: Phishing messages pretend to be from banks, shops or coworkers.
questions.tip: Phishing: they cast bait and hope you bite.

questions.q: What is two-factor authentication (2FA)?
choices: Using two passwords on one site
A second proof of identity, like a code, on top of your password
questions.explain: Even if a password leaks, the second factor blocks the thief.
questions.tip: Something you know plus something you have: your password plus a code from your phone.

questions.q: Which second factor is generally the most secure?
choices: A code sent by text message
questions.explain: Hardware keys resist phishing; texts can be intercepted and security answers guessed.
questions.tip: A physical key in your pocket beats a secret anyone could look up.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of a password manager?
choices: You can use a unique, strong password for every site
questions.explain: You only remember one strong master password.
questions.tip: One master key to a safe full of unique keys.

questions.q: Which is a red flag in an email?
choices: Urgent pressure to click a link and "verify" your account
questions.explain: Urgency and links to log in are classic phishing tactics. Logos are easy to fake.
questions.tip: Urgent plus link equals stop and think.

questions.q: Before clicking a link in an email, what should you check?
choices: Where it really goes, by hovering or long-pressing it
How many words the email has
questions.explain: Link text can say one thing and go somewhere else.
questions.tip: Hover before you go.

questions.q: Why install software updates promptly?
choices: They fix security holes attackers already know about
They always make the computer faster
questions.explain: Many attacks target known bugs in out-of-date software.
questions.tip: Updates are patches on a leaky boat.

questions.q: A caller says they are tech support and asks to remotely access your computer. What should you do?
choices: Let them in so they can fix it
Hang up and contact the company using an official number
questions.explain: Real companies rarely cold-call; scammers use remote access to steal.
questions.tip: You call them; they do not call you.

questions.q: What is ransomware?
choices: Malware that locks or encrypts your files and demands payment
questions.explain: Good offline backups let you recover without paying.
questions.tip: Ransomware holds your files hostage.

questions.q: Which password is stronger?
questions.explain: Length matters more than swapping letters for symbols, and P@ssw0rd is on every attacker's list.
questions.tip: A long passphrase is a fortress; P@ssw0rd is a tent with a sign on it.

questions.q: What is the 3-2-1 backup rule?
choices: 3 backups a day, 2 days a week, 1 month total
3 copies of your data, on 2 kinds of storage, with 1 kept offsite
questions.explain: Multiple copies in different places survive device failure, theft and fire.
questions.tip: 3-2-1: three copies, two types, one far away.

questions.q: Is a cloud sync folder a full backup?
choices: Not by itself: deletions and ransomware can sync too, so keep versioned backups
questions.explain: Sync mirrors changes, including mistakes. Version history or separate backups protect you.
questions.tip: Sync is a mirror: it copies your mistakes too.

questions.q: Which image format supports transparent backgrounds and lossless compression?
questions.explain: PNG keeps every pixel exactly; JPG is lossy and has no transparency.
questions.tip: PNG for pictures with no background; JPG for photos.

questions.q: What is a CSV file?
choices: A plain-text table with values separated by commas
questions.explain: CSV is Comma-Separated Values; spreadsheets open it easily.
questions.tip: CSV: Commas Separate Values.

questions.q: What is a ZIP file?
choices: An archive that bundles and compresses files
questions.explain: Zipping makes files smaller and easier to send as one.
questions.tip: A ZIP is a suitcase you sit on to close.

questions.q: Which attachment from an unknown sender is most dangerous to open?
questions.explain: .exe files are programs that run with your permissions.
questions.tip: .exe means execute: it does things, not just shows things.

questions.q: Roughly how many megabytes are in a gigabyte?
questions.explain: A gigabyte is 1,000 MB; its binary cousin, the gibibyte (GiB), is 1,024 MiB.
questions.tip: Kilo, mega, giga: each step is about a thousand times bigger.

questions.q: What does a file extension like .docx or .pdf tell you?
choices: What type of file it is
questions.explain: The extension tells the computer which app opens it.
questions.tip: The extension is the file's last name: it tells you its family.

questions.q: Why save a finished document as a PDF to share it?
choices: It looks the same on almost any device
It is always smaller than any other format
questions.explain: PDFs preserve layout and fonts across systems.
questions.tip: PDF is a printout you can email.

questions.q: How do you know your backups actually work?
choices: Check that the backup drive is plugged in
Restore a file from them now and then
questions.explain: A backup that has never been restored is only a hope.
questions.tip: Test the parachute before you need it.

questions.q: What does Ctrl+C (Cmd+C on a Mac) do?
questions.explain: It copies the selection to the clipboard.
questions.tip: C for Copy.

questions.q: What does Ctrl+V (Cmd+V on a Mac) do?
questions.explain: V sits next to C on the keyboard, and pastes.
questions.tip: V looks like a funnel pouring the copy back out.

questions.q: What does Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on a Mac) do?
questions.explain: Undo reverses your last action.
questions.tip: Z is the last letter: it takes you back from the last thing.

questions.q: What does Ctrl+F (Cmd+F on a Mac) usually do?
choices: Find text on the page or in the document
questions.explain: Find jumps to matching words.
questions.tip: F for Find.

questions.q: What does Ctrl+A (Cmd+A on a Mac) do?
questions.explain: It selects everything in the current area.
questions.tip: A for All.

questions.q: What does Ctrl+S (Cmd+S on a Mac) do?
questions.explain: Save often to avoid losing work.
questions.tip: S for Save: tap it like a nervous habit.

questions.q: On Windows, what does Alt+Tab do?
questions.explain: Hold Alt and keep pressing Tab to cycle. On a Mac, Cmd+Tab switches apps.
questions.tip: Alt+Tab is flipping between TV channels.

questions.q: In most web browsers, what does Ctrl+Shift+T (Cmd+Shift+T on a Mac) do?
choices: Reopens the tab you just closed
questions.explain: It is a lifesaver after closing a tab by accident.
questions.tip: T for Tab, Shift for "bring it back."

questions.q: Why does restarting a computer often fix odd problems?
choices: It clears memory and restarts stuck programs
questions.explain: A fresh start clears out glitchy states that build up over time.
questions.tip: A restart is a good night's sleep for your computer.

questions.q: What character starts a spreadsheet formula?
questions.explain: Typing = tells the spreadsheet to calculate.
questions.tip: Equals means "work this out."

questions.q: A1 is 2, A2 is 4 and A3 is 6. What does =SUM(A1:A3) give?
questions.explain: 2 + 4 + 6 = 12. The colon means "from A1 through A3."
questions.tip: The colon is a "through": A1 through A3.

questions.q: What does =AVERAGE(2, 4, 9) give?
questions.tip: Average: add them up, share them out.

questions.q: B2 is 59. What does =IF(B2>=60, "Pass", "Fail") show?
questions.explain: 59 is not 60 or more, so the false value is shown.
questions.tip: IF(question, yes answer, no answer).

questions.q: What does the $ do in $A$1?
choices: Keeps the reference fixed when the formula is copied
questions.explain: An absolute reference does not shift when you fill or copy the formula.
questions.tip: The $ pins it down like a thumbtack.

questions.q: The formula =A1*B1 in C1 is copied down to C2. What does it become?
questions.explain: Relative references shift by the same amount as the copy.
questions.tip: Relative references move along with the formula, like a shadow.

questions.q: What does =COUNTIF(A1:A10, ">5") do?
choices: Counts cells in A1:A10 greater than 5
questions.explain: COUNTIF counts cells that meet a condition; SUMIF would add them.
questions.tip: COUNTIF counts, IF they pass the test.

questions.q: What does the error #DIV/0! mean?
choices: A formula divided by zero or an empty cell
questions.explain: Check the cell you are dividing by.
questions.tip: You cannot share cookies among zero friends.

questions.q: What does =MAX(3, 9, 4) give?
questions.explain: MAX returns the largest value.
questions.tip: MAX is the tallest kid in the photo.

questions.q: What is XLOOKUP or VLOOKUP used for?
choices: Finding a value in a table and returning a matching value from another column
questions.explain: For example, look up a product code and return its price.
questions.tip: Lookup is reading a menu: find the dish, read across to the price.

questions.q: A1 is "Ada" and B1 is "Lovelace". What does =A1&" "&B1 show?
questions.explain: & joins text, and " " adds a space between.
questions.tip: & is the glue stick for text.

questions.explain: An f-string fills in the variable inside the braces.
questions.tip: f is for fill-in: braces are the blanks.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: sum adds every number in the list.
questions.tip: sum is the calculator tape at the bottom of the receipt.

questions.explain: 19.99 x 3 = 59.97, and round(..., 2) keeps two decimal places.
questions.tip: round(x, 2) is for money: two places after the point.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: milk, then eggs (each on its own line)
questions.explain: Looping over a dictionary gives its keys, in the order they were added.
questions.tip: A for loop over a dict walks through the labels, not the contents.

questions.q: What does "pip install requests" do?
questions.explain: pip is Python's package installer.
questions.tip: pip is the app store for Python.

questions.q: Why use "with open('notes.txt') as f:" to read a file?
choices: It closes the file automatically when the block ends
It makes the file read faster
questions.explain: The with block cleans up even if an error happens.
questions.tip: with is a door that closes itself behind you.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: split("-") makes a list of 3 pieces: "2026", "10", "13".
questions.tip: split is scissors cutting at every dash.

questions.q: What type of value does input() return?
choices: A string (str), even if the user types a number
questions.explain: Convert it with int() or float() before doing math.
questions.tip: input always hands you words; turn them into numbers yourself.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: max is 75, min is 68, and 75 - 68 = 7.
questions.tip: The range of numbers is highest minus lowest.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The format ",.2f" adds a thousands comma and exactly two decimals.
questions.tip: Comma for thousands, .2f for cents.

questions.q: What does this print?
choices: An error message and the program stops
questions.explain: The except block catches the ZeroDivisionError, so the friendly message prints instead.
questions.tip: try is the trapeze act; except is the safety net.
